Strong empirical results at tested scale: 71.6-81.6% iteration reduction and 1.27× slowdown vs. 4.24×+ for baselines; basis rotation restores scaling laws
Rigorous theoretical analysis with convergence bounds (Theorem 2.3) showing multiplicative interaction between delay τ and misalignment C

Comprehensive experimental ablations including basis approximation quality, update frequency, weight stashing variations, and computational overhead analysis
weaknesses: Significant gap between problem scope and experimental validation: paper claims issue is critical for 100+ stages but only tests up to P=32; maximum model size 1B (modern LLMs are 7B-405B); no validation at production scale

Core assumptions not quantitatively validated: block-diagonal and Kronecker-factored Hessian structure claimed 'empirically supported' but no empirical characterization of how well these hold in transformers or degradation when violated

Restrictive theoretical assumptions (coordinate-wise ℓ∞ smoothness, β₁=0) with loose convergence bounds that don't provide actionable guidance on when basis rotation is necessary; the (1,1)-norm proxy for misalignment lacks empirical validation of correlation with actual convergence

Limited experimental scope: single task (language modeling), single architecture (transformers), relatively short training runs, no benchmark evaluation (e.g., perplexity), no comparison of interaction with other parallelism strategies (tensor/data parallelism)
Computational overhead under-characterized: power iteration cost, memory cost of eigenvector storage, and scaling behavior to large models not analyzed; basis update frequency sensitivity limited

Incremental methodological novelty: basis rotation builds heavily on recent optimizers (SOAP, GaLore); main contribution is diagnosis and application to async pipeline parallelism rather than new techniques

Theoretical-practice gap: spiral loss landscape (Section 2.2) is synthetic; no empirical proof that (1,1)-norm predicts slowdown in real transformers; convergence bound doesn't guide when the (1+τ) delay factor becomes prohibitive

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Gradient staleness scaling with pipeline depth (5.81× slowdown) is a practical concern for LLM training
Clear logical structure: Progresses systematically from problem identification to root cause to solution
Multi-modal evidence: Combines empirical observations, theoretical analysis, and LLM experiments
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements across pipeline depths (76.8% fewer iterations on 1B models)
Practical solution with multiple strategies: Provides 1st/2nd order and unilateral/bilateral options with tradeoff analysis
Thorough experimental evaluation: Includes ablations on approximation quality, weight stashing robustness, and computational efficiency
weaknesses: Theoretical justification is incomplete: The connection between basis misalignment (measured by (1,1)-norm) and delay sensitivity is assumed rather than rigorously proven; Theorem 2.3 recovers known asynchronous SGD bounds without novel insights

Circular reasoning in the main argument: Defines basis misalignment by small (1,1)-norm, shows basis rotation minimizes this norm, but never proves that reducing (1,1)-norm improves robustness to delay

Synthetic validation insufficient: Figures 3-4 use simplified landscapes (quadratic, spiral) rather than validating on real neural networks; no direct measurement of Hessian properties before/after rotation on actual models

Restricted experimental scope: Models limited to 95M-1B parameters, pipeline depths to P≤32 (paper claims 'tens or hundreds' needed), training evaluated over only 250 iterations with batch size 8—convergence measured too early

Key assumptions unvalidated: Kronecker factorization and block-diagonality assumptions (critical for Theorems 3.1 and D.5) are stated as 'empirically supported' without direct evidence on tested models

Limited novelty: Basis rotation and similar curvature-aware strategies already exist (SOAP, GaLore); the contribution is mainly identifying basis misalignment as a factor in delay sensitivity, which is incremental

Computational cost not fully analyzed: Power iteration, QR decomposition, and weight rotation overhead every 10 iterations on small-scale experiments (95M); scalability to truly large models (>1B, P>100) unclear

Alternative explanations not excluded: Delay sensitivity could arise from momentum interactions, loss landscape evolution, or other factors; no isolation of basis misalignment as the primary mechanism
Baseline tuning concerns: Delay Compensation baseline (DC) performs poorly (Figure 16), suggesting suboptimal hyperparameter selection; limited comparison with other recent second-order methods
Experimental design issues: Weight stashing introduces O(P) memory overhead confounding the comparison; learning rate search over only 3 values; batch size 8 with no gradient accumulation is atypical

Rigorous theoretical analysis: Theorem 2.3 shows multiplicative interaction between delay τ and basis misalignment C; Theorem 3.1 justifies basis rotation under Kronecker structure
Comprehensive experimental validation spanning 95M-1B parameters with strong ablations across eigenbasis-estimation design axes, robustness tests, and practical considerations
Practical framework with implementable approximations balancing fidelity vs. efficiency; even simplified strategies (1st/unilateral) substantially outperform baselines

Comprehensive multi-layered empirical validation from synthetic examples (quadratic, spiral landscape) to real LLM pre-training with convincing results (81.7% iteration reduction on 3B model)

Principled solution design with multiple eigenbasis-estimation strategies offering flexibility and efficiency through Kronecker factorization and practical stage-aware allocation (29.2% additional speedup)

Thorough experimental analysis including ablations on basis approximation strategies (Figure 8), robustness without weight stashing (Figure 10), wall-clock efficiency (Figure 9a), and generalization to MoE architectures

strengths: Identifies and formalizes an important practical problem: gradient staleness degradation scales linearly with pipeline depth (5.81× slowdown at P=32), with clear practical significance for LLM training

Provides insightful mechanism diagnosis connecting basis misalignment (Hessian eigenbasis-coordinate mismatch) to Adam optimizer sensitivity under delay, demonstrated empirically across multiple settings (Figures 3, 4, 11)

Comprehensive theoretical analysis including convergence bounds (Theorem 2.3) showing multiplicative interaction between delay τ and misalignment measure C, with extension to stage-dependent delays and momentum (Theorems E.6, E.8)

Extensive empirical evaluation with multiple ablations on estimation strategies, model scales (95M-3B), and practical variants (stage-aware allocation). Demonstrates 81.7% iteration reduction at 3B scale and 54.3% GPU hour improvement
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Hessian-aligned coordinate rotation is well-established in K-FAC, Shampoo, SOAP, GaLore. Main contribution (application to async pipelines + stage-aware allocation) is incremental. Authors acknowledge sharing 'conceptual roots with several recent optimizers'

Marginal improvement over closely-related SOAP: Table 3 shows basis rotation (1.27× slowdown) vs SOAP (1.34×), a ~5% difference in the key metric, raising questions about whether gains come from basis rotation itself or careful hyperparameter selection

Significant gap between theory and practice: (1) convergence bound contains dimension factor d and large Hessian norm C, potentially loose; (2) no convergence guarantee for basis rotation algorithm itself; (3) stage-dependent delays require unknown per-stage misalignment values C²ᵢ for effective delay τ'; (4) main theorem assumes β₁=0

Restrictive and unvalidated assumptions: Theorem 3.1 requires exact Kronecker factorization (ℱ=A⊗B) with no error analysis; block-diagonal Hessian assumption relies on unverified citations; S=1st uses weak proxy E[G]E[G]ᵀ

Limited experimental scope undermines practical claims: (1) Virtual GPU stages (4 stages/GPU for P=32) don't reflect real distributed training dynamics—actual delays and communication costs differ; (2) only decoder-only Transformers tested, no encoder-decoder or vision; (3) maximum 3B scale is small relative to modern 7B-405B+ models; (4) no wall-clock time on actual multi-GPU setups

Hessian approximation quality underexplored: (1) No numerical analysis of ‖H - ℱ‖ or empirical Fisher factorization error; (2) power iteration convergence to true eigenvectors not analyzed; (3) basis update frequency (freq=10) chosen arbitrarily with limited sensitivity analysis; (4) Figure 8 shows unpredictable gaps between estimation strategies

Comparison with related work incomplete: SOAP is the critical baseline (both do basis rotation) but receives minimal discussion of algorithmic differences. Muon/Scion underperformance unexplained. Comparison with preconditioned methods lacks depth

strengths: Clear identification and analysis of basis misalignment as root cause of delay sensitivity in asynchronous pipeline parallelism, with compelling empirical motivation (5.81× slowdown) validated across multiple settings (synthetic spiral loss, real LLM training, oscillation visualization)

Strong theoretical contributions including convergence rate showing multiplicative interaction between delay τ and basis misalignment C (Theorem 2.3), stage-dependent delay analysis with insightful effective delay formula (Theorem E.6), and optimality result for bilateral rotation (Theorem 3.1)

Practical solution with substantial improvements: 71.6%-81.7% iteration reduction across model scales (95M-3B parameters) with flexible multi-axis design (approximation source × rotation geometry) enabling fidelity-cost tradeoffs

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple strong baselines, extensive ablations (eigenbasis strategies, update frequency, robustness without weight stashing), additional validations (validation loss, MoE, preconditioned optimizers), and direct empirical confirmation of core claims (oscillation dampening, Hessian norm reduction)

Excellent presentation with clear progression from intuition to theory to practice, effective visualizations (Figures 3, 4, 11), and thorough 40-page appendix with detailed proofs and experimental details enabling good reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: all experiments on OpenWebText with decoder-only Transformers, single task (language modeling), models capped at 3B parameters; generalization to other domains, tasks, and larger models (7B-405B) remains unclear

Insufficient validation of critical assumptions: block-diagonal Hessian and Kronecker factorization are essential to efficiency but only cited as 'empirically supported'; no direct empirical validation provided; missing sensitivity analysis for assumption violations

Theoretical analysis has limitations: (1,1)-norm characterized as 'proxy for basis misalignment' but relationship to actual alignment not rigorously established; dimension dependence could be loose for high-dimensional problems; 'linearized trajectory stability' argument assumes small gradient noise without formal characterization

Practical overhead and implementation barriers: memory overhead 0.06-0.83 GB per matrix becomes significant at scale; requires optimizer modification limiting adoption in existing frameworks; interaction with other optimizations (checkpointing variants, quantization) unclear

Modest differentiation from SOAP: Table 3 shows only 5% performance gap (1.34× vs 1.27× slowdown); claimed distinctions are implementation details (accumulation space, basis update timing, power iteration vs SVD) rather than fundamental algorithmic innovations

Experimental design concerns: virtual stages on single GPU may disproportionately affect overhead-intensive methods; limited learning rate search (3 values); validation loss shows substantial noise without statistical significance testing; no wall-clock time comparisons in main text
